old_title: Stock market today: Dow, S&P 500, Nasdaq futures fall as US-Iran war escalates, inflation jitters return
new_title: Stock market today: Dow, S&P 500, Nasdaq edge higher as bond yields pause climb
old_text:
Stock market today: Dow, S&P 500, Nasdaq futures fall as US-Iran war escalates, inflation jitters return
US stock futures edged lower in premarket trading on Wednesday as rising oil prices and bond yields sent ripple effects across markets.
Futures on the Dow Jones Industrial Average (YM=F) fell 0.1%, and S&P 500 (ES=F) edged lower by 0.2%, while contracts for the Nasdaq-100 (NQ=F) slipped 0.5%, extending losses after a losing day on Wall Street.
Stocks got off to an unsteady start in September as an escalation in the war in Iran caused Brent (BZ=F) crude oil prices to jump above $95 per barrel. On Tuesday, President Trump threatened to hit Iran "much harder" if the nation retaliates against a barrage of airstrikes launched on Tuesday.
The latest flare-up in hostilities has amplified fears of rising inflation, driving up bond yields in the process. On Tuesday, the 10-year Treasury yield (^TNX) rose to 4.79%, while the 30-year (^TYX) climbed to 5.27%, affecting a range of assets.
A trade standoff with Canada also remained in focus, with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney saying the US and Canada could resume trade discussions when Americans "stop throwing shade" and "start being serious" about negotiations. However, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent downplayed the idea that the US was in a trade war with Canada.
On Wednesday, ADP's private-sector hiring data will offer clues about the health of the labor market after job openings appeared frozen, providing insights into what Friday's monthly jobs report may show.
Earnings from Broadcom (AVGO) and Snowflake (SNOW) are also on the docket on Wednesday.
new_text:
US stocks gained on Wednesday as a rally in oil prices stalled and a Fed official tempered expectations that a Fed rate hike in September would be certain.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI) rose by about 0.6%, while the S&P 500 (^GSPC) climbed by roughly 0.5%. The Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC) floated 0.4% higher after a losing day on Wall Street.
Stocks recovered from earlier losses as oil prices pared gains, offering some relief amid the reescalation of the war in Iran. Brent (BZ=F) crude oil futures continued to trade near $95 per barrel, while WTI crude (CL=F) held near $90 per barrel. On Tuesday, President Trump threatened to hit Iran "much harder" if the nation retaliates against a barrage of airstrikes launched on Tuesday. Iran has said it is targeting US military bases in Jordan and Bahrain.
Market sentiment also improved after New York Fed President John Williams told CNBC that there were "no clear signs right now" that a September rate hike would be needed to bring down inflation.
Williams also suggested that the rise in bond yields could be due to a strong economy rather than a run-up in inflation expectations. On Wednesday, the 10-year Treasury yield (^TNX) remained at 4.79%, its highest level since 2023, while the 30-year (^TYX) held at 5.27%.
On Wednesday, ADP's hiring data showed the US private sector added 38,000 jobs in August, below economists' estimates of 47,000 positions added - a slightly bearish lead into what Friday's monthly jobs report may show.
Earnings from Broadcom (AVGO) and Snowflake (SNOW) are also on the docket on Wednesday, with both set to report after the closing bell.
- Ines FerréStocks climb as Treasury yields ease, oil holds steadyStocks climbed, snapping a two-day losing streak on Wednesday as long-dated bonds eased slightly and the dollar weakened. The Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI) ticked up by 0.6%, while the S&P 500 (^GSPC) rose by about 0.5%. Meanwhile, the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC) gained roughly 0.4%. Oil prices remained elevated near $95 per barrel, but investors shrugged off rising bets that the Federal Reserve will increase rates at its September policy meeting.
- Grace O'DonnellDivide deepens over how much oil is getting through the Strait of HormuzYahoo Finance's Ben Werschkul reports: This Monday in the Strait of Hormuz was either a great or terrible day for the global economy, depending on whom you ask. Ship-tracking service Kpler reported that "traffic declined sharply," with just five ships crossing on Monday, the same day that the US and Iran exchanged fire for the first time in a month. The data platform documented a mix of official ships as well as shadow vessels using concealment tactics. Yet the picture from the Trump administration couldn't have been more different, with Energy Secretary Chris Wright saying in a CNBC interview that over 17 million barrels of oil passed through the waterway on Monday. Wright called it a record since the beginning of the conflict.
- Ines FerréOil hovers above $95 but stocks edge higherOil prices edged higher on Wednesday, but stocks also rose in a reversal of the prior session. The three major averages were up at least 0.4% as Brent crude (BZ=F) rose roughly 1% to hover past $95 per barrel. West Texas Intermediate crude (CL=F) also climbed 1% to trade around $91 per barrel. Treasury yields eased slightly during the session, helping lift stocks and putting the S&P 500 on pace to snap a two-day losing streak. The movement is a reversal of prior sessions in which rising oil prices sent yields higher in anticipation of elevated inflation.
- Grace O'DonnellGoldman Sachs warns investors to expect lower returns over the next yearOne of Goldman Sachs' top equity strategists warned that investors should expect more gradual stock market returns over the next 12 months after strong gains in the last year. "We should acknowledge that the S&P 500 and indeed other equity markets around the world have had a phenomenal return over the course of the last year and year to date," Goldman Sachs chief global equity strategist Peter Oppenheimer told Yahoo Finance's Brian Sozzi in an exclusive interview on Opening Bid. "So we've already had a lot of good returns behind us. We would expect lower returns from here." Sozzi noted that Oppenheimer has a loyal following on the Street for his many prescient stock calls over the years. In the next year, Oppenheimer said stock returns will remain "decent" but below the double-digit gains investors have seen recently. "In most cases, we're talking about mid- to high-single-digit [percentage] returns over the next 12 months, lower than we've been seeing in every region in the last 12 months," Oppenheimer added. "But still, you know, relatively decent so long as economic growth continues. That's our expectation."
- Jake ConleyPalo Alto Networks is putting on an 'M&Asterclass,' says Deutsche BankPalo Alto Networks (PANW) is putting on an "M&Asterclass" with its acquisition strategy, Deutsche Bank Brad Zelnick said, adding that the company is differentiating itself through its approach to cybersecurity. A strong fourth quarter finish and fiscal-year 2027 guidance "reinforce[s] the company's position as the leading cybersecurity consolidator at what increasingly looks like a meaningful AI-driven demand inflection," Zelnick wrote on Wednesday, reiterating his Buy rating. "We believe the quarter materially speaks to management's credibility as an acquirer and integrator," he added. Shares were trading down by roughly 10% after the company reported earnings on Tuesday. Idira (formerly CyberArk) and Chronosphere, two companies Palo Alto previously acquired, are proof points of Palo Alto's strategy, Zelnick said, as both are "scaling faster than their prior standalone trajectories and performing ahead of initial expectations." So-called observability ARR has more than doubled to $500 million since Palo Alto closed its Chronosphere acquisition, while integration strategists for the company remain three to six months ahead of plan. Idira, meanwhile, has "generated over 400 shared leads and more than 200 new-logo wins from PANW's installed base," Zelnick wrote. "We view the combination of accelerating platform adoption, better-than-expected performance from Idira and Chronosphere, strong early traction with AI security and sustained cash-flow discipline as broadly supportive of our thesis," Zelnick wrote.
- Jake ConleyNvidia chief urges G20 leaders to not overly regulate AINvidia (NVDA) chief Jensen Huang urged G20 finance ministers to spur AI adoption to further their countries' economic growth. "Every single country needs to build infrastructure so you can support your own local economy," Huang said on Wednesday at the G20 meeting in North Carolina. "This is the great equalizer." Huang spoke alongside several other Big Tech and AI leaders, including SpaceX's (SPCX) Elon Musk and Meta (META) chief Mark Zuckerberg. The tech leaders are pressing G20 nations to adopt what's been dubbed the "Carolina Principles," which guide that governments shouldn't create new regulatory bodies that would slow down AI's build-out and usage. On Wednesday, Huang pushed for narrow regulations on AI and said that governments should leave companies to develop guidelines around AI instead of setting policy. "The technology is in its formative stages, and the advice that I would have is to regulate practical and actual harm, and not regulate theoretical and hypothetical harm," Huang said. "Every single company has to take it upon themselves to develop the technology safely." The biggest risk for nations that regulate AI, Huang said, is "being left behind."
- Jared BlikreGold keeps meeting traders halfwayGold has been trading very technically lately. And the level that keeps showing up is about as simple as it gets: the halfway back. Markets rarely go straight up or down, and after a big move, technical traders often watch to see how much of it gets retraced. The simplest marker is the 50% retracement - the exact middle of the move, or halfway back. Start with the big downswing in gold this year. Gold futures (GC=F) closed at 5,508.6 on January 29 (marked 1 in the chart), then fell to 4,048.7 by July 16 (2). Halfway back is 4,778.7 - the classic 50% retracement, marked by the red dotted line. Technicians often lump that level with Fibonacci retracements, even though 50% isn't actually a Fibonacci ratio. The idea is less mystical than it sounds: after a big move, traders want to know how much ground the market can win back. Gold rallied hard in August. But the rebound ran into that halfway-back zone. Futures reached 4,755 on August 25, just shy of 4,778.7, and reversed (3). Adding to the setup, its RSI, a momentum gauge, was in "overbought" territory. Now the same trick is working in reverse. The rally from the July 16 low to the August 24 closing high puts its halfway mark at 4,373.3 (4). Gold fell almost exactly there on Tuesday, touching 4,369.7. It opened Wednesday at 4,377.2, briefly traded below the level - and buyers showed up. That's technical analysis in its simplest form: Mark a level, watch what price does when it gets there, and adjust from there.
- David HollerithBofA says more of its customers are betting online, and Gen Z is driving the boomOnline betting is growing increasingly popular in America this year, with younger generations leading the charge. The latest evidence comes from Bank of America customer data showing that roughly 5% of its customers used a sports betting or prediction-market platform in July, up 40% from the beginning of 2026. The number of people making their first payment to a betting platform in June and July was more than three times the January levels, according to a Bank of America Institute report. The surge came as this summer's FIFA World Cup kicked off in the US, and prediction markets platforms have introduced a wave of new products. The growth is overwhelming from younger customers, Bank of America research finds, with Gen Z and millennials accounting for a respective 48% and 40% of online betting activity. Without being able to account for funds left on these platforms, the bank's transaction data gives a less optimistic picture of how these bettors are performing. On average this year, customers received less than $0.75 back for every dollar they moved to these platforms. Even Gen Z, which recovered the most cash of all customers, remained well below break-even, according to the report. The data arrives as the lines between online gambling and investing appear to be increasingly blurred and hotly debated. A recent survey from Betterment found that More than half of Gen Z adults ages 18 to 29 put money they had intended to invest for retirement into sports betting over the past year. An earlier Bank of America survey from March found 20% of respondents view sports betting as a type of investment, with Gen Z roughly twice as likely to see it that way.
- Grace O'DonnellFed's Williams says it's not clear whether the Fed has to take further action on inflationBets that the Federal Reserve would raise interest rates in September pulled back slightly after New York Fed president John Williams told CNBC that he believes inflation expectations are well-anchored and that a September rate hike isn't a certainty. Traders still expect 66.2% odds of a rate hike, come Sept. 16. "I think that we have to wait and see," Williams said. "There's no clear signs right now whether monetary policy currently is sufficient to make sure we bring inflation back to target in the next year or two, or whether you need to see further action to do that." Williams noted that recent inflation data has been encouraging, "but again we can't just look at a month or two. We've got to get a full picture and look at all the different pieces of information we have." Williams also noted that he doesn't see dysfunction in the bond market, per CNBC, despite the recent run-up in global bond yields. He tied the rise in Treasury yields to "a strong economic outlook fueled by big investments in AI and data centers and technology in general." "I think it's not really about financial conditions affecting the economy. It's more about the economy affecting financial conditions," he said.
- Jake ConleyChevron stock flat as investors digest news of $7 billion Venezuela investmentChevron (CVX) shares held mostly flat after the opening bell as investors digested news that the US oil major is set to invest more than $7 billion in expanding its presence in Venezuela. The announcement from Chevron, the only US oil company that has continued to operate in Venezuela over the past several years, marks the largest financial commitment yet by a US company in the country since the US removed the prior leader, Nicolas Maduro. Chevron's investment, which grants it additional acreage in Venezuela's Orinoco Belt oilfields, is intended to double production to roughly 600,000 barrels per day, the company said Tuesday. The news out of Chevron comes after the announcement that the US government will take a major equity stake in a wide swath of Venezuela's oilfields under a deal with the private company North American Blue Energy Partners. The deal, which will see the Pentagon's Office of Strategic Capital take a 35% equity stake in NABEP's parent company, will give the US State Department the right to buy 20% of the oil produced from NABEP's current and future fields at the cost of production, or with no markup. The deal also grants the US the first opportunity to purchase the other 80% of NABEP's production.
- Jake ConleyUS stock market splits at the opening bell on WednesdayThe US stock market opened Wednesday's trading session on unsteady footing as investors digested new waves of conflict in Iran and an early read on US employment in August. The Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI) ticked up by 0.5%, while the S&P 500 (^GSPC) rose roughly 0.1%. Meanwhile, the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC) lost roughly 0.1% to extend losses from Tuesday. Oil prices steadied on Wednesday morning after contracts on Brent crude (BZ=F) and US benchmark WTI crude (CL=F) both briefly touched their highest prices seen in more than a month. Driving the price action was another round of strikes between the US and Iran, expanding the return to direct conflict between the two nations in roughly a month. Data on the US private sector from payrolls provider ADP showed US private employers added 38,000 jobs, missing expectations and offering a bearish set-up for Friday's marquee nonfarm payrolls report.
- Jake ConleyOil prices steady after hitting monthly highs as US launches new round of strikes on IranOil prices steadied on Wednesday morning after the US and Iran exchanged another round of strikes, lengthening the first return to direct conflict between the two nations in roughly a month. Futures on Brent crude (BZ=F), the international benchmark, ticked down by roughly 0.4% to hold above $94 per barrel, while those on US benchmark WTI crude (CL=F) steadied just below $90. The two benchmarks ticked up to their highest prices in more than a month earlier in the session, reaching $97.04 on Brent and $92.29 on WTI contracts. The US military late Tuesday night launched a new round of strikes targeting "air defense sites, radar systems, maritime assets and facilities, mine laying capabilities, and communications sites" inside Iran, per US Central Command. US military leadership said the strikes were in retaliation for attempts by Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps to threaten through the Strait of Hormuz. Iran quickly thereafter claimed it had begun a "decisive operation" against US military sites in Jordan and Bahrain, per the state-affiliated Tasnim news agency. The renewal of conflict between the US and Iran, now roughly four days deep after a month of quiet, has brought the specter of energy-driven inflation back to the forefront, with a critical Fed decision only weeks away. The resumption of violence also comes only two months out from the US midterm elections, with the White House under increasing pressure to find a way to end the war. President Trump said late Tuesday night that he is "not trying to force Iran to the negotiating table." "I couldn't care less if they sign a worthless, to them, agreement," the president wrote. "I like our position now much better, with almost total control of the Hormuz Strait, and their economy totally collapsing. They are just playing out the inevitable. When are the Iranian people going to rise up and fight?"
- Jake ConleyUS private sector added 38,000 jobs in August, ADP saysThe US private sector added 38,000 jobs in August, according to data provider ADP, marking the slowest pace of job creation since January in another preview for investors before Friday's nonfarm payrolls report. The ADP figures for August fell from July's revised 46,000 jobs added, and underperformed economists' expectations of 47,000 jobs - a slightly bearish read on the state of hiring. Education and health services led job creation for the month, with 45,000 jobs created. The construction, leisure, and hospitality sectors also saw strength. The manufacturing sector led losses, in a move that will be watched for potential signals on the state of the AI infrastructure build-out. "Job-stayers" saw wages grow 3% year over year, flat from the previous month, while pay for job changers edged down to 4.7% from July's 4.8% year over year growth. "To understand hiring patterns, you have to look deeply into where pay growth is accelerating, where it's slowing, and for whom," said Nela Richardson, chief economist of ADP. "Once-predictable wage growth has been overtaken by the complexities of demographic change, persistent inflation, and AI's effects on jobs."
- Grace O'DonnellThe biggest unanswered question in Trump's Venezuelan oil deal: Where will the $100 billion in funding come from?Yahoo Finance's Ben Werschkul reports: President Trump's highly touted oil deal in Venezuela will require what all sides agree is about $100 billion in capital investment over the coming years to build the infrastructure needed to get the energy out of the ground. Yet while many aspects of the deal have been clarified, it's not clear where all that money will come from to fulfill Trump's ambitious promises in what he's calling the biggest oil deal in world history. The funding issue has emerged as perhaps the central unanswered question about the US government's plans for this major slice of Venezuela's oil fields, which geologists estimate holds approximately 65 billion barrels of oil - a massive quantity, but only about one-fifth of Venezuela's entire reserves, estimated at 303 billion barrels.
- Ines FerréDell stock surges on record orders for AI serversDell Technologies (DELL) stock surged as much as 10% in extended trading. The maker of laptops and servers raised guidance and posted record revenue and adjusted earnings for its fiscal 2027 second quarter amid a booming AI server business. The company said it booked a record $60.9 billion in AI server orders and exited the quarter with a record $95 billion backlog. Dell Technologies said it also saw growth in its traditional servers, networking, and storage businesses. The company posted record revenue of $47 billion, up 58% year over year. Earnings per share came in at $6.34, up 273% from a year ago. Adjusted earnings rose 203% to $7.04 per share. "With AI momentum accelerating and our opportunity expanding across the portfolio, we're raising our full-year FY27 revenue outlook by $25 billion to $192 billion, up nearly 70% year over year," said Jeff Clarke, CEO of Dell Technologies, in the company's earnings release.
- Grace O'DonnellGood morning. Here's what's happening today.Economic data: MBA mortgage applications, week ended Aug. 28 (-1% previously); ADP employment change, August (+46,000 expected, +44,000 previously); Factory orders, July (+0.6% expected, -0.3% previously); Durable goods orders, July final reading (+1.1% expected, +1.1% previously) Earnings calendar: Broadcom (AVGO), Snowflake (SNOW), Hewlett Packard Enterprise Company (HPE), NetApp (NTAP), Five Below (FIVE), Brown-Forman Corporation (BF-A, BF-B), FuelCell Energy (FCEL) Catch up on some top stories you might have missed overnight:
- Grace O'DonnellGlobal bond yields surge as oil prices fuel inflation worriesGlobal bond yields jumped on Tuesday as the latest hostilities between the US and Iran reinforced inflation expectations and bets that the Federal Reserve will opt to hike interest rates in September. The Wall Street Journal reports: The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield rose to 4.798%, the highest since January 2025, according to LSEG data. The U.S. two-year Treasury yield rose to 4.369%, which would be its highest settlement also in 19 months, reflecting rising bets on an interest rate increase by the Federal Reserve in September. One-year ahead U.S. inflation expectations, as measured by derivative markets, have crept up to 2.5% from less than 2% in the past couple of weeks, according to LSEG. The 10-year Japanese government bond yield crossed 3% to hit a 30-year high. The 10-year German Bund yield reached 3.364%, unseen since 2011. In the U.K., the 10-year gilt yield rose to 5.255%, its highest since 2008, while the 30-year gilt yield rose to levels unseen since 1998. "Global bonds are facing a perfect storm of rising inflation fears, driven by higher energy prices, which are in turn raising rate hike expectations," Leon Ferdinand Bost, analyst at Metzler said. "At the same time, fiscal concerns are back at the forefront and together with heavy supply are weighing on the long end," he said.
